newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: C&W welcomes more Singapore handphone competition.
newsitem.headline: C&W welcomes more Singapore handphone competition.

text.p: British Telecommunications giant Cable & Wireless (C&W) said on Thursday it welcomed competition in the Singapore mobile phone market and would try to drive down costs to maintain its margins.

Ross Cormack, C&W's Asian regional director for mobile phones, told Reuters the Singapore government's announcement on Wednesday that it would licence one or two more cellular operators from 2000 had been long expected.

C&W and its majority-owned subsidiary Hong Kong Telecommunications each own 15 percent of MobileOne (M1), which will become Singapore's second mobile phone operator on April 1, competing with the current monopoly, Singapore Telecommunication Ltd (SingTel).
The other partners in MobileOne are both local companies, Keppel Telecommunications and Transportation and local newspaper monopoly Singapore Press Holdings, which each hold 35 percent.
From April 2000, there could be four mobile phone operators in Singapore, Communications Minister Mah Bow Tan announced on Wednesday.
"We have always known that competition would be coming. It was made clear at the time of the bid that there would be extra competition from 2000 onwards," Cormack said in an interview.

"So we welcome competition. As a sharheolder of M1, we look forward as M1 to demonstrating a tremendous capability in the market place through value of proposition and quality of service. We believe we can be very established by the time the competition materialises," he told Reuters.

Cormack noted that SingTel had cut its mobile phone charges in the run-up to the entry of MobileOne into the market and said he expected charges to continue falling as competition made operators more and more efficient.
This would, in turn, reduce margins. But he said costs could also be reduced in response.
"I think there is no doubt that competition has played a part and will continue to play a part," in reducing mobile prices, he said.
"As penetration increases in all countries, the average revenue per customer tends to come down and we must drive the costs to serve those customers. That's our job."
Cormack said the Singapore market for mobile phones was already large but could grow a long way before it reached anything like saturation point.
According to the Telecommunication Authority of Singapore there are roughly 14 mobile phones for every 100 people in the city-state, up from 8.45 per 100 two years ago.
Cormack said he accepted industry estimates that this rate could rise sharply to between 28 and 40 per 100 over the next five to 10 years.
"I think they are reasonable expectations. It depends on meeting the market demand," he said. "This a market where people need to stay in touch on a personal basis. That is a tradition of culture."
"This is certainly a very small market in world terms but it is a very sophisticated market with an incredibly fast-growing GNP (gross national product) per capita."
